utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before the witness is brought in, let me say that today, although normally we would take the first break at 3.45, we will work until 4.00 and resume at 4.45, and the purpose of that is to allow the Judges to discharge other functions. Today we have a videolink witness. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is calling VG-119 via videolink, and the witness will be handled by Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. As Your Honours know, this witness is -- has a pseudonym and facial and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I would like to go into closed session to introduce the witness' pseudonym at this point. May we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when you say "sometime after that we left again; my mother-in-law, number 094," your former sister-in-law, can you recall the day or the month that you left for Strgacina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Around the 22nd or 23rd of May. Perhaps even earlier on, around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you set out on foot, or were you in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We took a bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you eventually reach Strgacina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, we did. My husband and my father-in-law remained in Dusce, and some days later they followed us across the woods, and eventually they reached Strgacina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did there come a -- you just mentioned that your husband, your late husband, and father-in-law joined you, so at that point the family was together. Do you recall the date that you were all together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: The 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Strgacina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: For two days, all of us. And then my father-in-law proposed that we go and stay in his -- at his brother's place in Belgrade. And then we started out and headed in the direction of Priboj. We met up there with my mother-in-law's relatives who put us up at their home. We had some coffee, and we had something to eat. We were about to get some rest, but then two soldiers knocked on the door wearing something that resembled the uniform used by the former JNA, telling us that we had to leave Priboj and that we couldn't travel on to Belgrade but, rather, we had to return to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: When -- when -- when my father-in-law heard that, he was off to look for a taxi driver, and he found Mr. Drago, who at the time had a red van that he used to drive people around. We all got into that van - meaning myself, my father-in-law, my mother-in-law, my younger sister-in-law, and then 094 - and we were off to Visegrad. We took the path across Bijelo Brdo, and we didn't go through Strgacina anymore. As soon as we reached Bijelo Brdo, we found several armed soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, I need to stop you, please. Thank you. You mentioned that you all got into the van, "meaning myself, my father-in-law, my mother-in-law, my younger sister... and then 094." Was your husband also in the van with you, your late husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: My husband -- yes, yes, my husband. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So on your way to Visegrad, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. We were pulled over by a group of armed soldiers. They asked us where we were headed, and we said, "To Visegrad." One of them knew my husband and said that it wasn't a good idea to go there, that there were all kinds of things going on there, that we should turn off and go somewhere else. My father-in-law was a good man at heart, but he was also a little hard-headed. He didn't believe that anything bad would happen to us, so he was adamant that we should travel on to town, all the way to Dusce. So we did, and then Drago said that he would drive us as far as Dusce. When we returned to Visegrad, near the Mehmed-Pasa Sokolovic bridge, three cars blocked our path carrying armed soldiers. One of the vehicles disgorged Milan Lukic, a person my husband knew. Also leaving one of the vehicles was Dragana Secerovic who was another person from Visegrad, and I knew her too. She was a hairdresser. They all left their vehicles, and then the remaining soldiers left their vehicles, and Milan Lukic ordered us to leave our vehicle, too. Dragan was the first person he approached, the taxi driver, and then asked him --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Stop, please. Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please find out also whether she also knew Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at the time you say Milan Lukic exited one of the vehicles, did you personally know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. My husband said that when he came out. They were the same generation, and my husband knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about these cars, what colour or what kind of vehicles they were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: The car driven by Milan Lukic was red. The other two were also red. The one driven by Milan Lukic was a Passat. It was a red Passat vehicle. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Had you ever -- excuse me, sorry. Had you ever seen this red Passat prior to this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. Yes. There was this lady who owned a grocers shop in town, and she had bought it just before the war erupted. But that lady, too, was killed, and then her two daughters were saying later on that their mother had been taken away and killed by Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, other than the two persons that you named, Dragana and the hairdresser and Milan Lukic, how many other persons were there that got out of the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many, but I would reckon four or five other persons at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Then you -- then you said Milan Lukic came up to the van, and what, if anything, did he say to anyone in the van?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: He spoke to Drago. He wanted to see our ID, and he provided those, and then the other man realised that we were Muslims, and then he said, "Drago, why are you driving these balija around? Why aren't you driving your own people around?" But he remained silent. Then he ordered us to leave the vehicle, which we did. We were now outside the vehicle, and then Milan Lukic and Dragana walked up to us and started frisking us. They took my husband's wedding ring away, and then they asked him for money. And then they walked up to my father-in-law; they took away his watch. My husband gave them 200 German marks, which was all the money he had on him. He kept the rest of the money in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but they never looked for it, so that's where the money stayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter missed a word that you just used. I'm going to ask you to repeat that. "He kept the rest of the money," and what did you say after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did have other money on us, so we hid the money in our bras, we, the ladies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell me, while this was going on, how far away were you from Milan Lukic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: A metre, a metre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what time of day was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: It was daytime. It might have been about 11.00 in the morning. It was before noon. It certainly was before noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did any of the other soldiers say anything to your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. It was past noon. Friday, past noon. It was just before 4.00 in the afternoon. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's okay, Witness. My next question was: Did you hear any of the other soldiers saying anything to your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. They were all armed. They were all standing there. Milan Lukic was holding a rifle slung over his soldier, the finger at the trigger all the while as he was standing there, rifle on shoulder and finger on the trigger. And then he took my husband's shoes off -- rather, he ordered him to take his shoes off, and he looked at the soles. Then they marched us back into the vehicle. Milan Lukic ordered that -- ordered us to get back into the vehicle and drive back to wherever our homes were. One --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And -- go ahead. Finish your -- what you were going to say, and then I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Dragana entered the car with us, with my group, with myself, my husband, my father-in-law. She turned the automatic rifle on us, and she said -- rather, she told Drago to drive to Dusce. We set off. Milan Lukic and the other soldiers entered their car, and they followed us in the direction of Dusce. When we reached the house where we live, everyone got out again. We were also ordered to get out, which we did. Milan Lukic then said, "You women, go into the house, and you two," my father-in-law and my husband, had to go with them to be questioned. So they got into the car, but my husband got into one of the cars, and my father-in-law got into another car. I asked them whether we could say goodbye to each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And let me just back up a minute, if you don't mind going a little bit slower. Do you know in which car your late husband got into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: He got into Milan Lukic's car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And who was driving that car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Milan Lukic was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And whom did you ask if you could say goodbye to your husband?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Objection; leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked Milan Lukic and Dragana Secerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just for the record, I said I was allowing the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when you asked this question, did you get a response; and if so, from whom, and what did the person say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: When I asked them to say goodbye, Dragana said I couldn't because she wasn't able to say goodbye to her husband either, and he allegedly came to harm, and she did not allow me to say goodbye. My husband then got into the car that Milan Lukic was driving, and my father-in-law got into the second car. The last thing I can remember is seeing his hand on the car window. I think that was the last time I was greeted by him. I then lost consciousness; I fainted. When I came to, I was already in the house and they were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you take a minute. Madam Witness, have you ever seen your husband since that time, or father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. Never after that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you ever learn of what happened to them? Were they ever found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: My father-in-law was found two years ago in Zepa. That's where Drina had taken him to, and he's been buried in Sarajevo. He was found dead. But my husband hasn't been found to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to move on to another topic now, Witness, okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. After this event, did you ever see Milan Lukic again; and if so, when is the first time that you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. That very same evening, after my husband and father-in-law had been taken away, someone knocked at the door. When we opened the door, Milan Lukic was there again with some of his soldiers. And I was then inside, but my mother-in-law opened the door. He asked for the wife of the husband, of the man whom he had taken away. I knew I couldn't hide. He said that I and code 904 had to go with him, which we did. We went to the car with him. When we got there, we got to the hotel, Banja, Vilina Vlas. I knew this hotel from before because I lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I need to stop you, Witness, if you don't mind. Sorry. Can you -- I forgot to ask you the date that this all happened, the taking-away of your late husband and now Milan Lukic coming to your house later. Do you recall the date that this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: The 29th of May. It was Friday at 4.00. That's when my husband was taken away. And Milan Lukic, on the 29th of May, returned to our house at 8.00 again, and he took me away as well as 904, code 904.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I believe -- if you look at the record, is it 904, or is it another number? I think it ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when he came to your house, did you -- what car was he driving, that you ultimately got into that car? Which car was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: The same car that he drove my husband away in. It was a red Volkswagen Passat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, you stated that he took you to the Vilina Vlas Hotel. What happened when you got to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: When we reached the reception on the first floor -- well, just in front of the reception, there was someone I recognised, a schoolmate. He was a little older than me, Sasa. They used to call him Sasa. I know him from school. When he saw me, he lowered his head. Milan Lukic ordered me to enter the lift. We went up and Sasa accompanied us. I don't know which floor we went to. I really can't remember, believe me. When we arrived up there, he ordered code 094 to go to a room with him, whereas Sasa entered another room with me. Time passed by. I spoke to Sasa. He said nothing would happen to me. At one point in time I heard some kind of a scream, a voice of some kind, and then after perhaps about half an hour or so, Milan Lukic appeared at the door to my room, and he told Sasa to go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I need to stop you. And when he ordered Sasa to go out, did Sasa say or do anything at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: When he was going out, I just saw how he touched Milan's arm. I don't know what I was thinking at the time, but I just saw him grabbing him by the muscle of his arm. Sasa then went out. When Milan entered the room, I asked him where my husband was. He said I'd find out. He asked me whether my husband had any weapons, where the weapons were. I said, "How can you ask his wife such a question? You saw that he didn't have any weapons on him when we were travelling." He didn't have weapons of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And after having -- did you have any other further conversation with Milan Lukic that you recall at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I said I thought he would help me. I told him I was pregnant, which wasn't true. While we were speaking to each other, the door was opened. Once more, Sasa was at the door and code 094, who was crying, she was shaking and crying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us -- can you tell the Judges why you said that you were pregnant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I thought Milan would abuse me, take advantage of me, and probably thanks to Sasa that did not happen because when he touched him, that certainly meant that he should not touch me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, after Sasa and 094 came to the room, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Milan Lukic ordered Sasa to take us back home, and we set off with Sasa again. We got into the car and set off home to Dusce that very same evening. About one hour later, we returned to Dusce at my mother-in-law's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: And on the way home, on the way home Sasa remained silent. He just looked at us and said nothing. When we arrived home, he returned and we entered the house, and we found my mother-in-law there and a younger relative. I told my mother-in-law that we had to leave the house because they would certainly return again, and that in fact happened. That night we left the house and set off in the direction of Bikavac. Earlier on, before reaching Bikavac, we spent the night in a yard. It was someone's yard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How did she get to Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I need to stop you. The Judge has a question, and try to remember that I need to ask you questions and then answer rather than just tell your whole story at once, if you could remember that, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wanted to find out, Witness, how did you get to Bikavac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That evening, above the house, between Bikavac and Dusce, there was a yard. It was cultivated. There was a plant that they would grow there. I don't know quite how to describe it -- beans, in fact, and we hid there in that field of beans, in that yard because it was night and we wanted to stay there until the morning because --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I need to ask you: How were you travelling at this time, by foot or by car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: On foot, on foot. It was a settlement, but we stuck to the woods. We followed a path lined by trees, by plum trees and so on. We went towards Bikavac. We reached this field of beans, this yard. We sat down there, and we waited for dawn to break. We didn't sleep there. We remained there, outside until dawn.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what happened at dawn? Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We headed off towards Bikavac on foot. We followed a path to Bikavac. When we came close to the houses, my mother-in-law said we should go to her friend's place, to her relative's place, Ramovic Baksa. She was a relative of my mother-in-law's. We arrived in front of the house. We knocked on the door; the door opened. Baksa came out. We asked her whether she could take us in. We told her what had happened, and she said she could. So we went into the house. She and her three daughters were there, her two sisters-in-law, and two grandchildren.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And now, can you tell me who you were with at this time? Was it still the same relatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, the same group: me, my mother-in-law, 094, and my younger relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at Baksa's house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We stayed there for a while, until Baksa said -- or told my mother-in-law that there was no more food and that they had to go to town to buy something. That was perhaps seven days after we had arrived. One morning they went to town, to Visegrad to buy some food for us. When they got to the supermarket in Visegrad, a soldier approached them and asked them who they were buying all this food for, and they said that they had a family in Bikavac. And this soldier took them to Nova Mahala, to the school called Hasan Veletovac school at the time, and they told them up there to go home and to bring all their family members to the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I need to stop you for a moment, Witness. Now, you're talking about "they went to the supermarket, and a soldier approached them and then took them to the school." Can you tell us who "they" and "them" is? Who were the people that went to the supermarket and ended up at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: My mother-in-law and Baksa Ramovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, after they were told to bring all their family members to the school, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: They returned to the house. They returned home. They said what had happened. They said that they had to take us to the school. We said we couldn't, we had to flee, that we had to leave Baksa Ramovic's house, and this is what we did. As soon as they arrived and told us what had happened - that was in the afternoon - we went off -- we set off in the direction of Visovca. We were looking for an abandoned house that we could use. We passed through the settlement, and we found accommodation in a house that was at the top of Bikavac; myself, my mother-in-law, my two sisters-in-law, Baksa and her daughters and sisters-in-law and the grandchildren, so this group found accommodation in that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can I ask you why it was that you did not want to go to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Well, because me and my sister-in-law and my mother-in-law had been through what we had been through, and we said that it wouldn't be good to go there. If we went there, the same thing would happen again, and who knows what else might happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, this house that you found that was empty, do you know who owned this house, or have you ever found out who owned this house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Later, I found out that this was Veljan's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And these -- can you tell me approximately how many people were with you in this house and whether these persons were a mixture of men, women, and/or children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We were all women. But that night, apart from the group that I have already mentioned -- well, another woman from Zupa joined this group that I had already mentioned. She had fled, and she asked us not to tell anyone that she was among us if someone started asking for a woman from Zupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us the date that you were at this house, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We spent some time in that house, perhaps ten days. We didn't go out of the house; we remained in the house. It was until the 27th of June that we remained there. In the evening at about 8.00 - well, it was still daylight - someone knocked on the door. Mrs. Dzemila Ramovic got up and opened the door. A group of Serbs entered the house. I recognised Milan Lukic whom I had already seen when he took my husband away and when he took me and 094 to Banja, to Vilina Vlas. So I saw him at the door again, and there were another five or six armed Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us, this -- how do you know that this was the 27th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: It was the 27th of June because I remember that -- that day. It was St. Vitus's day. That's why I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, did you notice if the men had arrived in a vehicle; and if so, what kind of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: At that time when they entered the house, you could hear music from the cars outside. We were sitting there. These armed men entered the house. They asked whether there were any women from Zupa with us. We didn't want to tell them anything about Ms. Hasa -- Mrs. Hasa, who was from Zupa. We said that there were no women from Zupa. They said, "No one should leave. We'll be back." They then left the house, Milan Lukic and his group of Serbs. They were armed. They left the house. When they left, the door remained opened. You could hear even louder music coming from the car. They were singing songs; for example, "Little girl, take your baggy trousers off." They were very vulgar songs. The music was very loud. We remained in the house. We didn't know what was happening outside. All we could hear was the music.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I need to stop you now. Thank you. And approximately how long were these men at the house this first time, this -- when you -- that you just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Not long. Between 10 and 15 minutes, so not very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And since it was summer, did you have the windows or doors open in the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Well, when we stayed in the house, we kept everything closed. We would even lower the blinds. So the windows remained closed, and the door of the house remained opened, and that's why we could hear this very loud music coming from their car.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after these men left, did anyone discuss the identity of any of these men, who they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I and my mother-in-law spoke about Milan Lukic, and Mrs. Baksa and my mother-in-law also spoke about Mitar Vasiljevic. They knew him from before. Mitar Vasiljevic. But the other people or men were not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you notice if any of them were wearing anything on their heads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. Mitar Vasiljevic was wearing a black hat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, what happened next in the evening, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We remained in the house when they left. We were just sitting there waiting to see what would happen to us. We didn't know if they were still there. All we could hear was loud music. They came back just before 10.00 that same night, the 27th of June, that same night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Again, they -- these same people returned, Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic, and the others who were with them. They came back to our house. When they came back, they said, "Why are you dressed like this?" That's what Milan Lukic was saying. My mother-in-law and Baksa had given us skirts that we put on over our trousers and some shirts and blouses, the sort worn by elderly women. They even given us kerchiefs to cover our faces, just to look as unattractive as possible. And Milan Lukic said, "It's as if the Serbs didn't know how pretty you were. What did these aunties do to you? What did they give you to put on?" And then he walked up to me and tore the kerchief off my head. I was seated in a corner of the house when he walked up to me, tore my kerchief off, and started pointing his finger at 094, at Zumra Ramovic, at me, and he said that we would be coming with them that same night. When he heard that, I pretended not to have heard this. I was so scared that I couldn't hear a single word. And then he spoke to me again and said, "Yes, you, too." And then what crossed my mind at the time was that perhaps I should faint, or at least pretend that I did, which is what I eventually did. I fell down from my perch. I fell down onto the floor, and I shammed that I was unconscious, which in fact wasn't the case. Milan Lukic walked up to me. He straddled me. He pulled me up by the shirt. The buttons shattered, and he told my mother-in-law to fetch some water. He doused me in some cold water, but I still pretended I was choking.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stop for a minute. I need to go back a bit to when these men entered the house again. Did all of them come in the house at this second time, or just Milan, or who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: They all went in, Milan Lukic and everybody else who was there the first time around --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what you just said. Would you please repeat it, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When they came again, they were all sweaty. They were dripping with sweat. They were dirty, too. The man with the hat had his shirt unbuttoned at the stomach so we could see his stomach through the shirt, and that's when Milan Lukic tore off my kerchief and ordered me to come with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, was it still -- was it still daylight outside, or what was the lighting like when you saw these men the second time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Our light was switched on. We didn't have the courage to switch it off when they left the house the first time around. We simply didn't dare switch the light off, so it remained on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So the light was on inside the house. Was there a light on the outside, by the entryway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: In the hallway, yes, there was one. Next to the door itself, there was a hallway and a light was on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after you pretended to faint and Milan told your mother-in-law to get water, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. My mother-in-law fetched some water, and they poured water on my body. He walked across my body and he said, "Fuck your Chetnik mother." I apologise. He said, "Go out, all of you," and he told my mother-in-law he would be back to see what was going on. And then one by one they started leaving the house. I opened one eye and peering, as I was, I saw Milan leaving the house, and he was the last. I covered my mouth with my hand. I started vomiting, and it wasn't before that that I actually fainted for real this time. My mother-in-law was trying to help me, but I was losing it. And they were -- they had left the house already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after the men left the house, did anything else happen that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Once we were back inside the house, because my mother-in-law had taken me from the bathroom through to that other room, we were just sitting there, talking about what we should do next and where we should go. We didn't dare leave the house. We thought that there would be no one around the house outside, but we didn't know for sure. So we decided to spend that night right there at the house. We were just sitting there. Soon it was midnight, and right after midnight, at about 2.00, we heard the sound of someone knocking at the door. My mother-in-law got up, went to the door, and opened it. As soon as the door was opened, we heard a woman scream at the door. We were frightened out of our wits because we thought that something had happened to her. Then we all walked towards the door and found Dzemila there and right in front of her, Zehra Turjacanin, who had obviously been burned. I didn't know Zehra at the time, but Dzemila did, and Baksa knew her too. They knew her personally, both of them, and they said, "This is Zehra." And she was brought to our house by a woman who left immediately. And we no longer met her, but we found Zehra there in a horrendous condition. Most of her upper body was burned to cinder, and so was her hair. It was, like, dry as a thistle. And then her arms up to her elbows, she was all burnt up, and she was a sorry sight, awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Did Zehra speak with you or anyone in the house at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: They spoke to us at the door. We asked her inside, but she refused. She said she had fled. There was another house further down the road right behind our house. She said over 70 persons had been assembled there, and then the house was set alight. She said she was just in time to jump out and save her life. She ran over to a creek in which she hid up until 2.00 that night, which was when she came to our door to tell us about this, to tell us about the burning of those people. She said that Milan Lukic was the one who had done that. We realised that this was the same time period, between 8.00 and 10.00, which tallied exactly with the time period that they were away from our house. We put two and two together ourselves, and we realised that no one else could have done it but those same people. I knew Milan Lukic, and then Zehra simply confirmed that Milan Lukic was the person who had done this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So at that point what, if anything, did you and the group decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't hear your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. My question is: At this point, after seeing Zehra and hearing what she had to say, what -- what happened next with you and the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We asked Zehra to come with us, but she refused. She didn't feel up to it, she said. She said she'd be off to the command at Bikavac, the Serb command, to surrender there and to tell them to either shoot her or do whatever they liked, whatever they pleased because she was all burned up and she couldn't go any further. That's what she ended up doing. We got together that night, and we decided that we had to leave. At the moment Zehra was off, we decided that we would be leaving, too, that we would have to be moving on. Baksa went back to get her two sons who were hiding behind the house in a bricked-up area. There were bricks lined up there and -- a bricked-up area, and Baksa bricked it up so that Ramovic Mujo and Ramovic Safet and her two sons and the late Osman Ramovic could hide in there. So these four men eventually joined us. Four men arrived at the house. So there was this group of ladies, those of us who were there plus the other seven, and we started out for Okrugla and Medjedja. We left --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When you left the house in Bikavac, did you notice anything as you were walking away from the house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. When we left the house and reached another house, the one behind us, we realised there was smoke rising out of that house and the house had burnt down, and there was a dreadful stench in the air of human flesh on fire. This was something horrendous. It was the ugliest thing I'd ever seen. I can't tell you how I felt. At the time, I was filled with fear and hatred at the same time, all sorts of emotions. We walked past the house. The house was still smoking, and there was this dreadful stench coming out of human flesh burnt alive. And then we headed across the woods towards Medjedja. We walked on down that path for five days, and then the last two days we had run out of food. We picked some cherries and some onions that we ate raw.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, would you please repeat what you just said. The interpreter is having difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We left that house, walked past the house that was still smoking with this stench of human flesh, burned, and then we spent the next five days travelling through the woods. The last two days we were out of food, so we ate raw onions and cherries that we picked on the way. Morning number five, and this had been an arduous journey across the woods, we saw a tunnel; and this was a tunnel through which you could reach the bridge over the Lim river and then take the road to Medjedja. We were out of the tunnel and there were Mujo Ramovic, Safet Ramovic, and Osman Ramovic. So we sent them ahead of us as some sort of sentry to see if there was anyone at the bridge. They were halfway across the bridge, nearly there, and they started waving back to us, signalling that it was safe for us to go. So we did, and we shouted for joy, but the Serbs were probably sleeping and now they were awake, so we started seeing soldiers sprouting -- popping up from behind the road wearing JNA uniforms. They said, "Stop right there." They stopped us. "Hands up." So we stopped. They searched us, searched our belongings. The four who -- or rather, the three who had remained back in the tunnel because the fourth man was with us, the ladies, Meho, he stayed with us, and those three went back yet again. Mujo and his brother and the cousin ran from the bridge from Strgacina, and they ran ahead, but we were at the midpoint of the bridge and they said, "Who are those three men who were at the -- who were on the bridge and who have just fled?" And we said that these were Mujo, Osman, and Safet. One of them then ordered me and Zumra Ramovic to go the way they had fled, and as soon as we realised where we were, that we should call out to them to surrender because unless they did they would kill all of us. We did just that. One of the Serbs was keeping us in the sights of his rifle all the time. He was standing at the bridge making sure we were well within his sights so that we couldn't run away. So then we went there, and I thought maybe they had turned off, and then up there I started calling their names out, "Mujo," once, twice, and then he answered. He said, "What's up?" And I said, "They're telling you to surrender. If you don't, they'll just kill all of us." Then I went back, and Zumra did as well. Once we were back, we walked up to the other soldiers there and our group, as well, and then I saw them look out over our shoulders. I said, "What are they looking at?" And then I turned around and saw Mujo right behind me. He was walking up to our group. And then they said, "Well, you, too, Ramovic, what on earth are you doing here?" And then they gave him half an hour to walk back to the woods and bring the other two back too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I need to stop you here, Witness. Sorry. Eventually -- were you taken into the custody by the Serb soldiers at this time; and if so, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. Mujo had gone on to fetch the other two, but he failed to reappear, and then they realised that he had put one over on them and that he would not be coming back. The Serb soldiers then started talking, and a TAM truck soon arrived. It was full of Serbs. There was another one that was empty, and that's where they put us, the ladies, those of us who were there, and they took us back to Visegrad, specifically to the Hasan Veletovac school.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the Hasan Veletovac school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Two days and that one night. That night and then the following day and then the half of that day, I mean, the day this whole thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then did you leave the school; and if so, who were you with you, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. I left the school with my mother-in-law, with 094, and my younger sister-in-law. We went back to Bikavac. We arrived at Safet Veljan's house. We stopped there, the same group, my mother-in-law, my sister-in-law, and I. We hid in the house for some time, spent some time hiding in the garden around the house, and then some time later, some days later, again, we left and were off to Okrugla with a group of ladies that we met somewhere behind this house. And we were off to Okrugla together. That night, or rather that evening, we were crawling. We spent a long time crawling because down the road from Bikavac there were guards and there was a searchlight illuminating the area, so we were off to Seganje and then off to Okrugla. That was the intention. So we moved slowly, and we didn't arrive until the next day when we reached free territory under the control of the Muslim army. And there were other people there in Okrugla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: When did you meet the Muslim army on your travels?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: This was sometime in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Specifically I'm asking, when you say you left the Bikavac house a second time heading for Okrugla and then you arrived with -- under the control of the Muslim army, so I just want you to tell the Judges, when you left that house the second time from Bikavac, where did you go, how long did it take you, and who were you with along the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: When I left the house at Bikavac, I walked with my mother-in-law, with 094, and my younger sister-in-law. Just behind our house, some way further up we met a group of other women. There was Fadila, her sister; her child, just a baby; and then Fadila's child, too, two children. So we joined them, this group of women, and we headed out together towards Seganje with Okrugla as our final destination. We walked that night. We crawled and we walked through the woods. It wasn't before the next morning where we reached Okrugla where we found the Muslim army. We knew that Okrugla was held by the Muslims. We had heard that there were still Muslims around in Okrugla.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you stay in Okrugla, or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We stayed for two days. At Bikavac we heard about Zehra, and her brother left with the army and went to Bikavac. He went there to look for her because we didn't know exactly what fate she had met. She had told us at the time that she was on her way to surrender. Then they went over to see if that was in fact the case, whether she eventually surrendered or whether something else happened. They found her at a lady's place. That's what they said when they returned. They found her at Bikavac. She was alone, this other lady, and when she saw Zehra, she -- they refused her to allow her to surrender. She held her back and hid her in her own home, so she helped Zehra. They picked Zehra up and literally stretchered her across to Okrugla. The night we arrived was when they brought Zehra -- the night of the day we arrived, they brought Zehra to Okrugla, which is when I saw her again. I spent this night with her helping the lady who was some kind of a nurse, and that was the lady helping her. I was giving them coffee, but her lips were burned, so she was unable to drink. I poured it down her throat, and I lit a cigar for her [Realtime transcript omitted, "and I lit a cigar for her"], but her lips were full of burns. It was really awful.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And during all this time, did you have a discussion, or did you hear any discussions about this fire at Bikavac and who might be responsible for this fire? Did you hear any names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that this question is calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And it's leading, as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not speculation. I'm asking if anyone said anything, and it's not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see no objection to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, Witness, my question was: During --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My apologies. We missed one part in transcript. She -- I think that witness mentioned cigarettes, and I cannot see in the transcript "cigarettes." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we have "cigarettes" in the transcript? Witness, did you say anything about cigarettes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think I have to remember every single detail every time I'm asked about these things? Yes, I did. I did mention cigarettes. But do I have to remember every single detail every time I'm asked about this? This cigarette, do you believe it to be something that important that I have to mention it every single time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. The cigarette was mentioned in the interpretation. The witness said she lit Zehra a cigarette.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, we're just asking -- some things aren't coming through. That's why we have to ask you some of these questions again. Now, the question I'd asked you before this was: During all this time that you were fleeing, did you have a discussion with anyone in the group or did you hear anyone in the group discuss who set this fire to the Bikavac house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: The night that I spent with Zehra, the next day there was an attack on Okrugla and we had to leave. They called him Hodza at the time. Zaim was his name; they called him Hodza. So he put together 730 men, some soldiers and some just ordinary people, and he took them to Medjedja. They were carrying Zehra's body through the woods, and the soldiers were saying that Zehra had spoken at some point and that she had said that Milan Lukic, his soldiers, and Mitar Vasiljevic were to blame for that. It's not like I was unaware of this by this time because I'd heard about it and I'd seen this myself. When those people came to our door, those were the same people who were now being blamed. I heard them talk. And then when we reached Medjedja, I heard that Zehra had been put up in some sort of a medical station, and I was just down the road from there in a different house. I would go over and see Zehra every day. I would just pat her on the head because that felt pleasant for as long as they didn't shave her head. But they did eventually at the medical station. They shaved her head. And then one day some journalists walked up to me. Zehra was being interviewed, and I listened in. They asked her if she knew who had done this to her, who had done this to all those people, and she said, "Milan Lukic, Mitar Vasiljevic," and then I heard her mention Sredoje Lukic's name. They asked for a description, whether she could remember what those people actually looked like, and she said she knew Milan Lukic personally. She knew Milan Lukic; that's probably what she meant. Sredoje was shorter than Milan, and his hair was fairer than Milan's, who was rather the robust individual. I had a flashback, and then it occurred to me that the third man involved had been Sredoje Lukic. The remaining three were still practically children, young men, very young. I didn't know who they were, and nor did she. That's what I heard at the time while Zehra was being interviewed. But that was the first time I heard her mention that. That was the first time I heard her mention Sredoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Is that the first time that you had heard his name mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And you don't know who the persons were who interviewed her, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I don't know. They said they were journalists, that they had come through Grepko, that it was for an interview when Zehra had been -- when had her hair had been cut. When it was over, they came for an interview with Zehra, although it was very difficult because she was still exhausted. But that's what she said then. I remember that quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We're almost through. I just have a few questions, and I'm going to change now to a different topic and ask you if -- during your proofing session this past weekend, did you review your prior statements that you had given in connection with what happened to you and what you observed during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, I read it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And did you recall giving a statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities in January of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. I gave a statement. The first time I gave a statement was in 1994. On that occasion, a statement was taken from me by someone who managed to irritate me a lot in one hour's time. It wasn't possible for me to give a full statement. I didn't complete my statement. I got up and left. I was still under a lot of stress; I was still very afraid. I don't know how to explain this. A young man came and said I would have to return to continue giving my statement on the following day. Another gentleman took my statement from me. It lasted for an hour or so. And that's the first time that I gave my full statement in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I haven't seen in any announcement from OTP that they will use any statement of this witness, so I'm a little bit confused with these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm not showing the witness any statement. I'm just asking her a question about her memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And Witness, do you recall during proofing being shown a statement appeared to be signed by you given to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities on the 21st of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it, and I was very irritated by it because I can't remember that statement. I didn't give that statement. I never gave such a statement because my statement has to do with Milan Lukic and the burning on Bikavac. I never gave such a statement to anyone. So this statement completely non-plussed me, although the signature does resemble my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall ever making any statements to anyone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Cepic, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting again. Could we have the full translation in transcript, if it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Full translation of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Witness mentioned -- could we repeat in B/C/S, please, Your Honour, with your leave. Witness mentioned [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. The interpreter translated it "as the statement completely non-plussed me." It was correctly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Last question, Witness. The things that are contained in that 21st November statement, do you ever recall making -- giving those items mentioned in that statement to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The statement I gave had to do with my husband, with him being taken away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Again, apologies, Your Honour, but we've been spending now time about the statements which are not announced in any list, neither in 65 ter submission related to this witness, so -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Sartorio, let us have the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I was just asking her about her recollection with regard to giving statements. I don't plan on showing the statements, introducing the statements. I just simply asked her the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What, then, was the purpose of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I presume that the Defence counsel are going to ask some questions about these statements, and I wanted to ask the witness some questions first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Well, we will -- are you through?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the adjournment now and resume at 4.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alarid, you are to cross-examine, but Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting. Your Honour, with your leave, I noted something. When the witness mentioned the name of my client, she was looking in some papers in front of her. Right now on the screen we see a couple papers. I don't know what kind of papers are in front of witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So what is the point you want to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that it is not allowed, any documents to be in front of the witness during the examination, except if some of parties tender something or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it all depends on the kind of document, Mr. Cepic, but I will ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, it has been observed that you have some papers in front of you. Can you tell us what those papers are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My code is on one of the pieces of paper, the code that you used to refer to me with; and the other paper bears the code of my sister-in-law, and this is a code that you use when referring to her and that I use when referring to her too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All of that is perfectly proper. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a reference from the court assistant. Is it necessary for me to turn off my mic every time following my question?

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You do not wish to be reprimanded, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It's happened too many times, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good afternoon, VG-119.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid, and I am the attorney for Milan Lukic, and I'd like to ask you a few questions. Can we do that today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to start basically where the Prosecution left off and ask you a few questions about statements you've given in this particular case. Do you recall how many statements you've given in total to either police officials, the Association of Women Victims of War, or the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. Four statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Because specifically I have a statement dated the 17th of January, 1994, and I believe you testified earlier that you reviewed that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And that statement is approximately eight pages, typewritten in Bosnian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And then based on the Prosecution's question, you also reviewed a November 21st statement, 1994, at the Gorazde centre, and you did review that, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I did but over the weekend. It was only last weekend that I read through that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you reviewed this with members of the Office of the Prosecutor at a proofing session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, because I couldn't read through my prior statements, but at that proofing session I read through all of my statements, and those statements also included the one you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And would you agree that in the 21st of November, 1994, statement that your signature appears at the bottom of all three pages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Although it looks like my signature -- well, there are certain differences. So I would say that it isn't my signature and that I didn't sign that statement. There are certain discrepancies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you in Gorazde in November of 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in reviewing the statement of 1994, would you agree that there are certain details that definitely relate to your -- your person, your family, and situations with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. I noticed that there were some details that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Including the -- your sister-in-law's name, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And your younger relative, who was 12 years old; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No, not 11 years old. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Samira -- Samira is the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, but she wasn't 11 years old. The child was at the time going to the 1st grade in school, so she was seven years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In 1992, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will move into private session if we're going to pursue that line of examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And may any previous mention be redacted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't mean to interrupt. I just -- there was a name mentioned by this witness and also by Mr. Alarid in this statement referring to a young person. I think that should also be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you also recall giving a statement around the 3rd of January, 2005, possibly to the women's victims -- Association of Women Victims of War?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And do you also recall giving another follow-up statement - sort of another proofing session, if you will - the 19th of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, what I'm going to focus on is basically the 1994 statement of 17th of January because -- the reason I ask you that -- or I would ask you, is it fair that your memory should be most fresh the closest to the incidents of which you testify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you expecting an answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I guess I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Ma'am, is it true that your statement -- or your memory is the most fresh the closest to the incident of which you testify?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. But when I gave that statement or on each other occasion when I gave statements, well, these are things that you can never forget because it's painful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, the first date that you indicate is the date that you could never forget, of course, is the 29th of May, 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I would like to get a little bit of background history, if you will, and it's part of our ongoing investigation, but you indicated that you were 19 years old in 1992; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And how long had you been married at that time? And maybe if I could ask you, what was your anniversary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I got married on the 19th of October, and I had been married for seven months, so in 1991. It was on the 18th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And where were you married?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: In the Repusevic village, near Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And were you married in a civil ceremony or a religious ceremony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: It was a marriage in the municipality that resembled all other municipal marriages. It was a normal marriage. At the time, there weren't any particular customs that one followed. We got married in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, do you recall when the Uzice Corps came to town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: In April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Were you one of the persons that was taken to the stadium, the football stadium and addressed by a Colonel Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you hear about that time when all the people were brought to the football stadium and addressed by the Uzice Corps and the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And because we've gotten information from other witnesses that literally thousands of Muslims were taken to the stadium and addressed by the colonel at the beginning of the Uzice Corps's occupation of Visegrad. You didn't hear about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So this wasn't something that any of your relatives discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. At the time, we were in Drinsko, Uzamnica, and Uzice. That's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was your husband ever arrested during the time that the Uzice Corps was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. My husband worked. He worked until the Uzice Corps withdrew. He worked in a furniture factory in Dusce.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so that was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: He was never taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so he worked in the Varda factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. When the Uzice Corps started withdrawing, by that time everything was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: When did the Uzice Corps start withdrawing, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I think it was towards the end of April or at the beginning of May. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, in your statement of 1994 you indicated that you got information that the White Eagles were terrorising Muslim people, and that's when you decided to leave. Who told you about the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Well, the people who lived there, men who knew more about this than the women, naturally. There were Muslims who lived there. There were men there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Isn't it true that before the 29th of May, 1992, you -- did you hear about Milan Lukic at all, or is that the first day that he came up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: That was the first time I saw him, but I'd heard about the Eagles, the fact that they were in town. They had started taking people away and raping women. But the first time I saw Milan Lukic was on the 29th of May, no earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And understanding that you did not know Milan Lukic before this date, that was strictly -- he -- your husband identified him that day; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because they were the same generation and he knew him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and that's kind of what I'd like to ask you about because from your testimony of what happened, it didn't seem like you had much time to discuss that because of the ride you took and the fact that your husband was soon taken away. When did you discuss Milan Lukic and where he was from with your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No, I don't think you understood what I was saying. I spoke to my husband once we had been pulled over and once we had been IDed, our ID taken from us. Once our documents had been looked at, my husband told me that the man in question was Milan Lukic. When Dragana got into the van with us, we were no longer able to talk to one another because she pointed her rifle at us. While Milan Lukic was IDing us, as he was in the process of IDing us, my husband said, "This is Milan Lukic." That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you stated --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: And that was the last word ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so you didn't get any history on where they knew each other from or how they knew each other in that short period of time; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: They were the same generation, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: By assuming that, what year -- what year was your husband's date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And he went to school in the Visegrad area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, I'd ask you to describe in as much detail as possible how Milan Lukic looked on the 29th of May, 1992. Could you first describe how tall he was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Quite tall, quite a tall man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How many centimetres, if you can estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: 180 perhaps. Around 180, but I can't really say. I was so scared. I didn't even dare look at him properly. He was quite tall. He wasn't fat or anything. He was rather corpulent. He was strong, and he was wearing camouflage and carrying a rifle every time I met him. Rifle was slung over the shoulder, finger on the trigger. That's it. I'm not sure if you want to know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What colour was his hair, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did he have any facial hair or distinguishing marks on his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. I don't know if there was a birthmark, perhaps, or some other distinguishing feature. But no moustache, no beard, clean-shaven. Like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: How was his hair cut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: He looked youthful, and he looked my husband's age.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was his haircut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Slicked back like this. The haircut was tidy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The camouflage, was it a specific colour, or was there a primary colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: It was camouflage, not the JNA but the camouflage kind, and I'd never seen it before then, but I did see it a number of times later on. This was the first time I'd set eyes on a uniform like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And when you say "camouflage," was it green or was it blue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But again, was there a primary colour green, or was the primary colour blue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: I really can't say, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Was it short-sleeve or long-sleeve?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Long. Long, the shirt and the trousers. That I do remember. Long sleeves, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the rifle, was it the kind that had a clip, like an automatic weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Automatic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, when this car pulled over and your husband was taken, would it be fair to say that you would blame Milan Lukic at that point if he arrested your husband for never seeing him again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm sure you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: All I -- all I saw -- everything I saw boiled down to the fact that he was the one in charge. When all the others were silent, he and Dragana were talking. He was the man in charge. When he spoke to Dragana, I realised what his role was because I noticed the tone that he took and the manner in which he did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And there was no more than a total of five other soldiers there, including Dragana? Is that about right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: There were Dragana and a number of other soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And was this Milan Lukic wearing anything on his head, a hat or an insignia of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. His other soldiers did have the Serbian caps with cockades, and there was one who was wearing a cross around his neck. I don't quite remember, but I think Milan Lukic's head was bare. He was in camouflage, and he was holding onto this rifle throughout that was slung over his shoulder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And again, this was an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And what then -- at the time that your husband and father-in-law were taken away, it was your understanding that they were to be taken to the police station for questioning, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: What I believed at the time was that they were being taken away for questioning, yes. It never crossed my mind at the time that what eventually happened to them might happen. However, an hour later after they promised they would bring them back, it began to dawn on me that they might never come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And -- but as far as you know, they may have been taken and dropped off with someone else at the police station, and then something could have happened to them after that? Could that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. I know that. I'm no fool. I saw it. I saw the way he behaved. I saw what he did. My husband got into his car, and off they were. No one else. The Eagles, Milan Lukic. No one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: But your father-in-law got into another one of the vehicles, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: True. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in fact, one of the vehicles had a police siren, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: It did. I can't remember, but yes, it was a siren, and they sounded the siren once I'd fainted, and then I was told that they drove through all of Dusce with the siren on. But I fainted as soon as the -- they were off. As soon as I saw my husband in that car, I fainted. So that's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Could you identify, or did anyone tell you which car had a siren?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: No. I couldn't do that at the time. My mother-in-law said that she could hear a siren once they were off, but I don't know where it was that they were off to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Can you describe the other two vehicles? And I ask you if -- in the context of were any of those other two vehicles a police car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Red, red, same as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So all three vehicles were red? Can you tell me the make and model of the other two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I do remember, the only thing I know is that the one in the middle was a Golf. I don't know about the third car, but there was no police car. There was no police car around. Three red cars. That's all. I don't remember the make of the third. I know about the Golf, the one in the middle, and the Passat that Milan drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, referring to your statement, after your husband's disappearance, you were taken to the hotel but you were not sexually assaulted, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Correct. I was not assaulted, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the one thing that Milan Lukic did question of you was the location of your husband's guns or if he had any guns, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he asked, but I'm grateful to Mr. Sasa because I think this would have developed differently had it not been for him. I think the original intention was something different altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you believe Sasa prevented this with a touch to Milan's arm, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes. I am certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, would it be correct, though, that during this time, this time of chaos and conflict, it would have been proper for soldiers to inquire of -- where weapons were, if nothing else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: He did ask. He did, although he saw that we were civilians and we were on our way out of all this chaos, but he still asked the question. Was there any need? My husband was unarmed. He was a family man, a working man. If we had known what would befall us, we would never have stayed in Visegrad. If we had seen this sort of thing coming, we would have left long before. We had the money. We were able to just up sticks and leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was Sasa's last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Aleksandar Rosic, I think. I'm not sure about his last name. We weren't classmates. I do know him from school, but I think he was one or two years ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the questioning regarding a possible weapon of your husband's only lasted a few minutes, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG-119
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps up to ten minutes, the whole thing, before Sasa showed up at the door again with 094 who was crying and shivering, trembling. And then on Milan Lukic's orders, we were driven back to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
